Lemma helps you learn geometry and solve problems. Let\'s take a quick tour to see what it can do!
Type a geometry problem or take a photo of it. Lemma shows you the answer, step by step.
Use the drawing board to make lines, circles and shapes. Tap any shape to see its size and angles.
Draw a flat shape, press Extrude, and watch it pop up into a 3D figure you can spin around.
Every theorem comes with a picture, a simple explanation, and a quick quiz to check what you learned.
Your solutions and drawings are saved here, so you can open them again anytime.
Tip: tap a point or line in the figure to see its measurements.

Add at least 3 points on the ground to extrude.
Tap the grid to drop points. Tap the first point to close the shape into a face.
Face created — press Extrude to make it 3D
Rotate the view so you look down at the grid, then sketch.
✅ Correct! Tap for the next question.
🎉 All correct! You\'ve mastered this theorem.

• Sum of angles is 180°.
• Pythagorean theorem: a² + b² = c².
• Area: ½ × base × height.
• Law of Sines: a/sinA = b/sinB = c/sinC.
• Law of Cosines: c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cosC.

• Sum of angles is 360°.
• Rectangle area: a × b.
• Parallelogram area: a × h.
• Trapezoid area: ½ × (a + b) × h.
• Rhombus area: ½ × (d1 × d2).

• Circumference: C = 2πr.
• Area: S = πr².
• Arc length: (angle/360) × 2πr.
• Sector area: (angle/360) × πr².
• Tangent is always perpendicular to radius.

• Prism volume: Base_Area × h.
• Cylinder volume: πr²h.
• Pyramid/Cone volume: ⅓ × Base_Area × h.
• Sphere volume: ⁴/₃πr³.
• Sphere surface area: 4πr².
When two straight lines cross, the angles opposite each other (vertical angles) are equal.
Two crossing lines make four angles. The pair that sits “back to back” across the crossing point are mirror images, so they are the same size. The two angles next to each other always add up to 180°.
∠AOC and ∠COB lie on a straight line, so ∠AOC + ∠COB = 180°. Likewise ∠BOD + ∠COB = 180°. Subtracting the shared ∠COB gives ∠AOC = ∠BOD. ∎

• Scissors, railway crossings and the letter “X” all show equal vertical angles.\n• In problems: knowing one of the four angles tells you all four — the equal one, and 180° minus it for the two neighbours.\n• Lets you find unknown angles without measuring.
If an angle is 45°, what is its vertical angle?
Two lines cross; one angle is 110°. What is the angle right next to it?
In an isosceles triangle (two equal sides), the two angles at the base are equal.
An isosceles triangle is symmetric. Fold it down the middle and the two equal sides land on each other, so the two base angles must match perfectly.
Draw the bisector AD from the apex to the base. Then AB = AC, AD is shared, and the split apex angles are equal, so △ABD ≅ △ACD by SAS. Hence the base angles ∠B and ∠C are equal. ∎
• Roof trusses, tents and bridges use isosceles triangles so both slopes match.\n• In problems: each base angle = (180° − apex) ÷ 2.\n• Reverse is also true — equal angles mean equal opposite sides.
If the apex (top) angle is 40°, what is ONE base angle?
A base angle of an isosceles triangle is 50°. What is the apex angle?
The three interior angles of any triangle add up to 180°.
Whatever shape a triangle has, its corners always use up exactly half a full turn. So if you know two angles, the third is locked in.
Through the top vertex draw a line parallel to the base. The two alternate-interior angles equal the base angles, and together with the apex angle they form a straight line of 180°. ∎

• Find a missing angle in navigation, surveying or design: third = 180° − (α + β).\n• Lets you check whether three angles can even form a triangle.\n• It is the foundation of almost every other triangle theorem.
Two angles are 50° and 60°. What is the third angle?
A right triangle has a 90° angle and a 25° angle. What is the third angle?
Any side of a triangle is shorter than the sum of the other two sides (a < b + c).
A straight line is the shortest path between two points. Detouring from A to B through a third corner C is always longer, so no side can ever reach the combined length of the other two.
The shortest distance between two points is the straight segment AB. Any path A→C→B is longer, so AB < AC + CB. The same holds for every side. ∎
• Instantly tells you whether three lengths can form a triangle.\n• Same “shortest path” idea powers GPS and network routing.\n• In problems: the third side lies strictly between |b − c| and b + c.
Two sides are 5 and 7. What is the MAXIMUM whole-number length of the third side?
Two sides are 5 and 7. What is the MINIMUM whole-number length of the third side?
An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles not next to it.

Extend one side of a triangle. The angle that sticks out is exactly as big as the two far corners added together — because that exterior angle and its neighbour make 180°, and so do the three interior angles.
Exterior angle + adjacent interior angle = 180°. The three interior angles also sum to 180°. Cancelling the shared adjacent angle gives: exterior = sum of the two remote interior angles. ∎

• A quick way to find an angle without first finding the third interior angle.\n• Used in star polygons and when tracking turning angles along a path.\n• Shows an exterior angle is always larger than either remote interior angle.
The two remote interior angles are 50° and 70°. What is the exterior angle?
An exterior angle is 110° and one remote interior angle is 45°. What is the other remote interior angle?
When a transversal crosses two parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal and co-interior (same-side) angles add up to 180°.

Parallel lines have the same tilt, so a line crossing both makes the same angle pattern at each crossing. Matching (corresponding) angles are equal, and two angles on the same side between the lines complete a straight 180°.

Slide one crossing point along the transversal onto the other. Because the lines are parallel, the figure maps exactly onto itself, so corresponding angles coincide and are equal. Co-interior angles are supplementary to equal angles, so they sum to 180°. ∎

• Railways, ruled paper and ladder rungs all make equal angles this way.\n• Lets you “transfer” a known angle across a parallel line.\n• In problems: equal corresponding/alternate angles; supplementary co-interior angles.
A transversal crosses two parallel lines. One angle is 65°. What is its corresponding angle?
Two parallel lines are cut by a transversal. A co-interior angle is 120°. What is the other co-interior angle?
In a parallelogram, opposite sides are equal, opposite angles are equal, and neighbouring angles add up to 180°.

A parallelogram has two pairs of parallel sides. Because the sides run parallel, each opposite pair stays the same length, opposite corners match, and any two corners sharing a side complete a straight 180°.
Draw diagonal AC. Alternate interior angles are equal (parallel sides) and AC is shared, so △ABC ≅ △CDA by ASA. Hence opposite sides and opposite angles are equal. ∎
• Drafting linkages, gates and pantograph arms keep their shape using parallelograms.\n• In problems: opposite sides/angles equal, neighbours supplementary, diagonals bisect each other.
One angle of a parallelogram is 60°. What is the neighbouring angle?
One angle of a parallelogram is 60°. What is the opposite angle?
The area of a triangle is S = ½ × base × height.
Any triangle is exactly half of a parallelogram with the same base and height. So take base × height and halve it. The height must be measured perpendicular to the base.
Copy the triangle and rotate it to join the original into a parallelogram of area base × height. The triangle is half of that, so S = ½ × b × h. ∎

• Estimating fabric for a triangular sail or the area of a triangular plot.\n• Any of the three sides can be the base — pick the one whose height you know.\n• In problems you can also work backwards to find a missing height.
Base 10, height 4. What is the area?
A triangle has area 30 and base 12. What is its height?
In a right triangle, the square of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the legs: c² = a² + b².
The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle. The squares built on the two legs add up exactly to the square built on the hypotenuse.
Place 4 copies of the right triangle inside a square of side (a+b). The empty middle is a square of side c. So (a+b)² = 4·(½ab) + c², which simplifies to a² + b² = c². ∎
• Screen/TV diagonals, ladder lengths, and the 3-4-5 trick for square corners.\n• Only works in right triangles.\n• In problems: find a missing side, or test whether a triangle is right-angled.
Legs are 3 and 4. What is the hypotenuse?
A right triangle has hypotenuse 13 and one leg 5. What is the other leg?
The segment joining the midpoints of two sides is parallel to the third side and half its length.
Connect the middles of two sides. That short segment runs parallel to the base and is exactly half as long, because it is a copy of the triangle scaled down by ½.
The midsegment and base form similar triangles with ratio 1:2 (two sides halved, shared included angle), so the midsegment is parallel to the base and half its length. ∎
• Measuring a distance you cannot reach, e.g. across a lake, using midpoints.\n• In problems: midsegment = base ÷ 2, and it splits the triangle into similar shapes.
The base is 24. What is the midsegment?
A midsegment is 9. What is the base it is parallel to?
The altitude to the hypotenuse satisfies h² = a_c × b_c, where a_c and b_c are the two segments it cuts on the hypotenuse.

Dropping a height onto the hypotenuse splits the right triangle into two smaller triangles that are copies of the original. The height becomes the “geometric mean”: its square equals the product of the two hypotenuse pieces.
The altitude creates two triangles similar to the original. From the proportion a_c / h = h / b_c we get h² = a_c × b_c. ∎
• Find a height when only the hypotenuse divisions are known.\n• h is the geometric mean: h = √(a_c × b_c).\n• Each leg is also the geometric mean of the hypotenuse and its adjacent segment.
The hypotenuse segments are 2 and 8. What is the altitude h?
The hypotenuse segments are 3 and 12. What is the altitude h?
In a right triangle, the median to the hypotenuse is half the hypotenuse (m = c/2).
The midpoint of the hypotenuse is the same distance from all three corners — it is the centre of the circle through them. So the median to that midpoint is just a radius, half the hypotenuse.
The circumscribed circle of a right triangle has the hypotenuse as its diameter, so its centre is the hypotenuse midpoint. The median equals the radius = c/2. ∎
• Finding the centre of a right-angled shape.\n• In problems: median to hypotenuse = half the hypotenuse, and all three vertices lie on one circle.
The hypotenuse is 18. What is the median to it?
The median to the hypotenuse is 7. What is the hypotenuse?
The three medians meet at one point (the centroid) and each is divided in a 2:1 ratio from the vertex.
Every triangle has a balance point. All three medians pass through it, and it sits twice as far from each vertex as from the midpoint of the opposite side.
Midsegments create similar triangles; matching them shows the intersection divides each median in a 2:1 ratio. ∎
• The centroid is the centre of mass — a triangular plate balances on it.\n• In problems: vertex-to-centroid = ⅔ of the median; centroid-to-midpoint = ⅓.
The short part of a median is 4. What is the whole median?
A median is 18 long. How long is the segment from the vertex to the centroid?
Parallel lines crossing two transversals cut them into proportional segments.
If several parallel lines cross two slanted lines, they slice both lines in the same ratio. Equal spacing on one line forces equal spacing on the other.
The parallels create similar triangles (equal corresponding angles). Similar triangles have proportional sides, so the intercepted segments share the same ratio. ∎
• Dividing a plank into equal parts with ruled parallel lines.\n• Scaling drawings and maps.\n• In problems: set up the proportion a/b = c/d and solve.
A line parallel to a triangle\'s base splits one side into 3 (top) and 6 (bottom). It splits the other side into 4 (top) and x. What is x?
Parallel lines cut one transversal into 2 and 4, and the other into 3 and x (same order). What is x?
The midsegment of a trapezoid is parallel to both bases and equals their average: m = (a + b)/2.
Join the midpoints of the two slanted sides. The segment is parallel to both bases, and its length lands right in the middle — the average of the long and short base.
A diagonal splits the trapezoid into two triangles. The midsegment is built from two triangle midsegments of length a/2 and b/2, so m = (a + b)/2. ∎
• Estimating the average width of a tapering field or beam.\n• In problems: simply average the two parallel sides.
The bases are 8 and 12. What is the midsegment?
The midsegment is 15 and one base is 10. What is the other base?
c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos(γ), where γ is the angle between sides a and b.
It is the Pythagorean theorem with a correction term. If γ = 90° then cos 90° = 0 and it becomes c² = a² + b². For other angles the extra term adjusts for how “open” the triangle is.
Drop an altitude to split the triangle and apply Pythagoras to both right pieces, substituting the projection b·cos γ. ∎
• Find the distance between two points from two distances and the angle between them (flight paths, surveying).\n• Works for any triangle, not only right ones.
a = 3, b = 4, angle = 90°. What is c?
a = 5, b = 8, angle = 60° (cos 60° = 0.5). What is c²?
a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C) = 2R, where R is the circumradius.
In any triangle each side is proportional to the sine of the angle facing it. The shared ratio equals the diameter of the circle through all three vertices.
Area S = ½ab·sin C = ½bc·sin A. Dividing by ½abc gives sin A/a = sin C/c, and so on for all sides. ∎
• Triangulation and GPS positioning.\n• Best when you know an angle and the side opposite it.
Side a = 10 and sin A = 0.5. What is the diameter 2R of the circumscribed circle?
a = 6, sin A = 0.5, sin B = 0.25. What is side b?
An inscribed angle is half the central angle that subtends the same arc.
An angle with its vertex on the circle “sees” an arc at half the size the centre sees it. So every inscribed angle standing on the same arc is equal.
Draw a radius to form an isosceles triangle. By the exterior angle theorem, the central angle is twice the inscribed angle. ∎
• Equal viewing angles in theatres and stadiums.\n• An angle inscribed in a semicircle is always 90° (Thales\' circle theorem).
The central angle is 80°. What is the inscribed angle on the same arc?
An inscribed angle is 35°. What is the central angle on the same arc?
From a point outside a circle, tangent² = (external segment) × (whole secant).
From a point outside a circle, the straight tangent touch-length, squared, equals the product of the near and far distances along any secant line through the circle. This is the “power of a point”.
The tangent-chord angle equals the inscribed angle, making the two triangles similar. Their proportional sides give tangent² = external × whole secant. ∎
• Distance to the horizon from a height (a tangent to the Earth).\n• In problems: solve tangent² = external × whole for the missing piece.
Tangent = 6 and external secant segment = 4. What is the whole secant?
Tangent = 8 and the whole secant = 16. What is the external part?
A circle fits inside a convex quadrilateral exactly when opposite sides have equal sums: a + c = b + d.
For a circle to touch all four sides, the tangent lengths from each corner must balance. That balance is precisely the condition that the two pairs of opposite sides add up to the same total.
Tangents from a point are equal. Summing the 8 tangent pieces that make up the 4 sides shows a + c = b + d. ∎
• Designing rounded inscribed fittings.\n• In problems: use a + c = b + d to find a missing side.
Sides in order are 5, 8, 7, x. What must x be for a circle to fit inside?
Sides in order are 9, 6, 4, x. What must x be for a circle to fit inside?
When two chords cross inside a circle, the products of their two segments are equal: a × b = c × d.
Cross two chords inside a circle. The crossing point cuts each chord into two pieces. Multiply the pieces of one chord and you get the same number as multiplying the pieces of the other.
The two triangles formed share equal inscribed angles (same arcs), so they are similar. Matching their sides gives a × b = c × d. ∎
• Another “power of a point”, now for a point inside the circle.\n• In problems: solve a × b = c × d for the unknown segment.
One chord is cut into 4 and 6. The other is cut into 8 and x. What is x?
One chord is cut into 3 and 12. The other into 6 and x. What is x?
In a cyclic quadrilateral, the product of the diagonals equals the sum of the products of opposite sides: d₁·d₂ = a·c + b·d.
For a quadrilateral whose corners lie on a circle, multiply the two diagonals together — you get the same total as adding up the products of the two pairs of opposite sides.
Pick a point on a diagonal that makes equal angles with the sides. The resulting similar triangles give two proportions which add to Ptolemy\'s relation. ∎
• Historically used to build the first trigonometric (chord) tables.\n• In problems: find a diagonal or a side in a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle.
A cyclic quadrilateral has a·c = 20 and b·d = 16. One diagonal is 6. What is the other diagonal?
In a cyclic quadrilateral a·c = 15, b·d = 9, and one diagonal is 4. What is the other diagonal?
If a line outside a plane is parallel to some line lying in the plane, then it is parallel to the whole plane.
If a line never meets a line that lives in the floor, and it is not in the floor itself, then it never touches the floor at all — it runs parallel to it.
Suppose the line met the plane. Then it would also meet the parallel line inside the plane — but parallel lines never meet. Contradiction. ∎
• Power lines parallel to the ground; a shelf edge parallel to the floor.\n• A line parallel to a plane shares 0 points with it.
How many points does a line parallel to a plane share with it?
A line outside a plane is parallel to a line inside it. How many points does the outside line share with the plane?
If two intersecting lines in one plane are parallel to two intersecting lines in another plane, the planes are parallel.
Two flat sheets are parallel if each contains a matching pair of crossing directions that line up. Once they do, the sheets never meet.
If the planes intersected, the intersection line could not be parallel to both crossing pairs — which is impossible. So the planes are parallel. ∎
• Floors of a building; shelves in a cabinet.\n• Parallel planes share 0 points.
How many points do two parallel planes share?
A cube\'s top and bottom faces are parallel. How many common points do they have?
A line is perpendicular to a plane if it is perpendicular to two intersecting lines in that plane; then it is perpendicular to every line in the plane.
To stand a pole truly upright, it is enough to make it square to two different floor directions that cross. Then it is automatically square to every direction in the floor.
If the line is perpendicular to two intersecting lines through its foot, then by the perpendicularity criterion it is perpendicular to their whole plane. ∎
• Flagpoles, table legs and skyscrapers standing vertically.\n• The angle between a line perpendicular to a plane and any line in the plane is 90°.
A line is perpendicular to a plane. What angle (in degrees) does it make with a line in the plane?
At least how many intersecting lines in a plane must a line be perpendicular to, to be perpendicular to the whole plane?
If a line in a plane is perpendicular to the projection of a slant, then it is perpendicular to the slant itself.
A slanted line casts a shadow (its projection) on the floor. A floor line that is square to the shadow is also square to the slanted line above it.
The floor line is perpendicular to both the projection and the vertical height, hence to their plane, hence to the slant lying in that plane. ∎
• Aligning slanted rafters and guy-wires.\n• In problems: switch perpendicularity between a slant and its projection.
A line in a plane is perpendicular to the projection of a slant. What angle does it make with the slant itself?
A line in a plane is perpendicular to a slant. What angle does it make with the slant\'s projection?
A prism is a stack of identical flat layers. Multiply the area of one layer (the base) by how tall the stack is.
By Cavalieri\'s principle, summing equal cross-sections of area S over height h gives V = S·h. ∎
• Water capacity of a pool; concrete in a beam.\n• Works for any straight prism, whatever the base shape.
Base area 20, height 5. What is the volume?
A prism has volume 84 and base area 12. What is its height?
A pyramid holds exactly one-third of the prism with the same base and height — the rest tapers away towards the apex.
A triangular prism can be sliced into three pyramids of equal volume, so each pyramid is ⅓ of the prism. ∎
• Volume of the Great Pyramid, tents and hoppers.\n• Remember the ⅓ factor compared with a prism.
Base area 30, height 10. What is the volume?
A pyramid has base area 12 and height 5. What is its volume?
The space diagonal of a cube with edge a is d = a√3 (so d² = 3a²).
To cross a cube from corner to corner you combine three perpendicular edges. Applying the Pythagorean theorem twice gives the long diagonal as the edge times √3.
A face diagonal is a√2 (Pythagoras). Combine it with the vertical edge a: d² = (a√2)² + a² = 3a², so d = a√3. ∎
• The longest straight object that fits inside a cubic box.\n• In problems: d² = 3a² for the space diagonal, and face diagonal² = 2a².
A cube has edge 2. What is the SQUARE of its space diagonal?
A cube has edge 5. What is the square of its face diagonal?
A cylinder is a prism with a circular base. Multiply the circle\'s area (πR²) by the height H.
A cylinder is a prism with a circular base. By Cavalieri\'s principle, V = S·H = (πR²)H. ∎
• Capacity of pipes, cans and tanks.\n• In problems the answer is often left as a multiple of π.
R = 2, H = 10. What is the volume divided by π?
R = 3, H = 5. What is the volume divided by π?
A cone is a pyramid with a circular base, so it holds one-third of the cylinder with the same base and height.
Using the pyramid formula with circular base area πR²: V = ⅓·(πR²)·H. ∎
• Ice-cream cones, funnels and piles of sand.\n• Remember the ⅓ factor compared with a cylinder.
R = 3, H = 10. What is the volume divided by π?
R = 2, H = 9. What is the volume divided by π?
A sphere\'s surface matches the side area of the cylinder that just wraps around it, and its volume is two-thirds of that cylinder.
Archimedes\' proof: the sphere\'s surface area equals the lateral area of its circumscribing cylinder; integrating that area yields the volume. ∎
• Material needed for a ball; fuel in a spherical tank.\n• In problems the answer is often a multiple of π.
Radius 3. What is the surface area divided by π?
Radius 3. What is the volume divided by π?
The lateral (side) surface area of a cylinder is A = 2πRH.
Unroll the curved side of a cylinder and it becomes a rectangle: its width is the base circumference (2πR) and its height is H, so the area is 2πRH.
Cut the side along a vertical line and flatten it. You get a rectangle of width 2πR and height H, whose area is 2πRH. ∎
• Label area on a can or bottle; paint for a pillar.\n• Total surface adds the two circles: 2πRH + 2πR².
R = 2, H = 5. What is the lateral surface area divided by π?
R = 3, H = 4. What is the lateral surface area divided by π?
